sentences.text: Japan's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as its specialist supplier and manufacturer: it holds a role in all ten strategic compacts, and 61 economies count it as their best-placed trusted partner somewhere in the chain.
Its exposure sits at the start of the chain: imported fuel, minerals it does not mine, and refined rare earths.

Its industrial effort should go into battery materials refining and battery components, where its anchors are among the strongest and allies need new capacity, and into extending its positions in EV drivetrains, wind components and nuclear fuel.
For minerals and wind materials it should depend deliberately on trusted producers, and its development cooperation can help developing partners add the battery and wind capacity allies lack.
At home, deployment is as pressing: nuclear, solar and wind power need to be built faster.
The high fence belongs around the rare-earth chain, fuel supply, and the control software that can command Japan's grid, batteries, inverters, turbines and vehicles.

The rare-earth chain from separation to magnets, where China holds 94% of world supply of rare-earth and battery-metal refining, which covers battery metals as well as rare earths, and trusted suppliers only 4%.
The supply of oil, gas and coal, which takes one to three years to rebuild.
The control software of grid, battery, inverter, turbine and vehicle equipment.
The answer is trusted supply, stocks and control of command paths, not self-sufficiency.

Catch Up in battery materials refining and battery components, among the best-anchored cases and with high need, where allies also need new capacity, and extend existing positions in EV drivetrain components, wind components, and nuclear fuel and reactor parts.
No Preserve call clears the evidence bar.
Keep specialist supply, from chip equipment to transformer steel, reliable for allies: an allied commitment, not a domestic fence.
Battery and EV minerals from trusted producers such as Australia, the United States and Canada, and wind materials, where allied supply falls short.
With developing partners, add trusted battery and wind capacity through development finance and offtake.
Accelerate nuclear, solar and wind power and gas networks, buying commodity hardware competitively from trusted suppliers, with security conditions on connected equipment.
Leave open wafers and PV cells, polysilicon refining and gas-plant equipment.

The table takes the capabilities where an acute route meets the assets Japan depends on most, with gas and coal together.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the magnets of EV motors and wind generators.
Japan has 9% of world exports of the refining step, and 20 economies have it as their best-placed trusted refiner.
China holds 94% of world refining supply and trusted suppliers 4%; it provides 47% of Japan's imports.
Rebuilding takes more than three years.

Trusted separation, metal and magnet capacity at home and with allies such as the United States and Australia, through co-investment and offtake; stocks until it qualifies; limits on adversary sources in critical uses, phased in.
Supply-chain need is 98 out of a hundred, and supply takes one to three years to rebuild.
The United Arab Emirates supplies 44% of imports; trusted suppliers hold 29% of world supply, and allied supply falls short.
Stocks sized to the rebuild time; capacity reservations with several trusted producers, such as the United States, Canada and Norway; demand-side substitution.
Gas use is an Accelerate deployment, and coal still fuels power; both are imported.
Australia supplies 39% of gas and 66% of coal imports; allied supply covers the need, but rebuilding takes one to three years.
Long-term and capacity-reservation contracts with trusted producers, such as Norway, the United States and Belgium for gas; stockholding obligations; stress tests.
Control software of grids, inverters and batteries
Firmware and grid-control software can command, update or disable equipment from abroad.
China supplies 77% of battery cell and pack imports, 48% of PV module and inverter imports and 51% of transformer and switchgear imports.
These are hardware shares for the steps that carry the control layers; the data do not measure who supplies the software.
Trusted-source and certification rules for firmware, communications and remote access; trusted vendors where control is built into the hardware.
Remote access to wind turbines and vehicles
Turbine controllers and connected-vehicle software reach energy assets and fleets from abroad.
China supplies 56% of imports under the wind turbines step's trade codes, which also cover cables, substations and transformers, and 47% of EV and charger imports.
These are hardware shares for the steps that carry the control layers; the data do not measure who supplies the software.
Limits on remote access and over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors; certified trusted control software and a replacement programme.
Reactor control and safety instrumentation and oil terminal control systems sit behind the same fence and take the same trusted-source rules.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
This is where Japan makes its real industrial choices, by asking whether a capability is worth having (Strategic Industrial Value) and how strong Japan is today (Competitive Position).

For Japan, Catch Up in components and assembly often means closing a gap to the frontier from a substantial base; in battery materials refining and wind turbines it means building from a low position.
No Preserve call clears the evidence bar.
Reactors and steam generators reads Preserve on low confidence, with a position (79) just above the top-quarter bar (75).
Battery cells and packs and EV and charger manufacturing sit just below the bar and read Catch Up, also on low confidence, and coal-plant components is flagged for review by the engine.
Battery materials refining is the clearest case for building: high value, a low position (19), three capability anchors and high confidence.
China holds 94% of world supply and trusted suppliers 4%, so trusted capacity is scarce for every ally.
Battery components is also well anchored: Japan holds 13% of world exports and has operating capacity behind them, and 8 economies have it as their best-placed trusted partner.
Yet 84% of its own imports come from China.
EV drivetrain components (60), blades, towers and nacelle parts (55) and nuclear fuel and reactor parts (61) extend positions Japan already holds, with high confidence.
Other Catch Up calls are weaker than they look, and this brief does not build on them:
Wind turbines: a position of 16 on a world supply share of 2%, in a step whose trade codes also cover cables, substations and transformers.
PV modules and inverters: moderate confidence, conventional modules read Watch, and the trade codes include machines for making wafers and chips.
Uranium conversion and enrichment: an inherited anchor (a strong position in the next step up the chain) and a world supply share of <1%, so trusted allied enrichment comes first.
Battery recycling: a single export-share anchor in a step whose trade codes are battery waste, scrap and residues, with no position measure.
Japan holds 0% of world supply in battery and EV minerals and the data show no credible pathway to scale it.
So dependence should be deliberate and spread across trusted producers such as Australia, the United States and Canada; allied supply covers the need.
In rare-earth and wind materials refining, allied supply sits in Germany, Belgium and Spain and falls short, so co-investment and offtake must add capacity.
Its rare-earth separation layer belongs to the High fence.

Low fence — what not to prioritize
A credible strategy also says what not to localize.
Watch is not a failure: affordable, diversified access matters more than domestic production, and for Japan it often marks positions that compete without help.
Wafers and PV cells, and polysilicon refining.
Supply-chain need for wafers and cells is low (32), and polysilicon refining is a large, commoditized yard worth at most a stated capability floor.
Wafers and cells rank among Japan's most protected steps in its own measures, but the trade codes include chip wafers and chip-machine parts, so some of that may be chip policy.
Gas turbines, LNG plant and their components.
Japan holds top-quarter positions (83 and 84) on modest need and low value; its makers compete for the gas build-out without a fence.
Grid metals refining and grid components.
Need is low in components (35) but high in grid metals refining (72), a large, commoditized yard; the position in components is in the top quarter (88).
Grain-oriented electrical steel reads Catch Up only by inheriting its step's position, while allies rely on Japan for transformer steel: a supplier role to keep reliable.

In the Allied Industrial Base analysis Japan combines capital & investment, specialized technology and scale manufacturing roles, and it ranks first among allies on its measure of strength (compacts with a specialist position, workstreams it bridges).
It supplies 21% of world exports or production of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, 28% of wafers and 11% of automatic controllers.
It holds a core seat in five compacts: Permanent Magnets & Drive Systems, Battery Materials & Cells, Solar Manufacturing, Grid Equipment & Conductors and Electric Vehicles.

It is the largest allied holder of wafers and PV cells (11%) and PV modules and inverters (9%), but those positions rest partly on chip equipment and wafers that share the steps' trade codes, so they overstate its PV output.
Minerals, refined rare earths, wind materials and fuel.
If China's supply stopped, as in the Decoupling scenario, Japan would lose US$14.5 billion a year of imports across the Allied Industrial Base basket.
New capacity at the best-placed allied hosts, led by Germany, would restore only about US$2.1 billion of it a year.

Under Managed Interdependence, the default scenario, Japan sits in the minimum coalition of 7 Sectoral Compacts (the finer units beneath the strategic compacts); under Decoupling, 14, in 11 of them as a demand anchor.
These bargains turn that exchange into a specialization partners can count on.

Japan's own supply chain supports 21 pairs with 12 partners across four steps, and the table leads with them: rare-earth and wind materials refining; battery materials refining; battery components; and wind turbines.
India, the Philippines and Viet Nam are lower middle income, so project preparation, infrastructure and skills come first.
Indonesia and Mexico are upper-middle-income economies, where finance, guarantees and offtake should lead.
India's case is the thinnest: a single export-share anchor and a Competitive Position of 0.
The Philippines also has a Competitive Position of 0, as do the other partners in its step, so its case rests on a share of world exports and operating capacity.

The last row rests on the allied gap alone, in a step where Japan's own call is a review case, as do many of the 28 allied-gap pairs, so the headline count overstates the pairs that rest on a settled Japanese call.

Battery materials refining is among the broadest strands, level with battery components: 7 developing economies, led by the Philippines and Madagascar, have credible pathways, and Argentina, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Malaysia already host new capacity commercially.

Thailand and Malaysia host its new capacity commercially, and no partner qualifies in minerals or fuels.
Another 29 pairs are commercial, where trade, offtake and investment fit better than aid.

Wherever the equipment is made, nuclear, solar and wind power and gas networks clear the Accelerate bar of 60.
Solar and wind rest on all three measures with high confidence, though system need drives them: demand adequacy alone (41 and 49) is below the bar.
The renewables target of 201 GW by 2030 compares with 133 GW installed in 2025, a shortfall of about 47 GW at the recent build rate.
Between 2020 and 2025, solar grew from 71.9 to 92.2 GW and wind from 4.1 to 6.2 GW; nuclear capacity was flat (33.1 to 33.1 GW).
High deployment priority does not imply high manufacturing priority.
Japan has Catch Up cases behind nuclear and wind, but deployment should not wait for them: equipment should come from whichever trusted supplier is ready.
Gas reads Accelerate on system need, as a firming fuel whose supply sits behind the High fence.
Clean hydrogen also reads Accelerate, but on a single indicator of low confidence, so it is a review case.
Battery storage, grid networks and EV adoption sit below the bar: worth watching, not forcing.

First, oil, gas and coal are Secure but rank at or below the middle among Japan's own recorded measures: that shows little industrial-policy attention, not missing stocks, so stocks and trusted contracts should be tested against the rebuild time.
Second, wind turbines read Catch Up with little recorded attention, but on a weak position, so attention belongs with components and partners.
Finally, solar deployment policy lags while protection concentrates on wafers and cells, a Watch step: effort should shift toward deployment.
Secure the rare-earth chain with allied partners
Build trusted separation, metal-making and magnet capacity at home, where the base exists, and with allied partners such as the United States and Australia through co-investment and offtake.
Hold stocks until that supply qualifies, and phase in limits on adversary sources in critical uses only as it does.
Hold fuel security through stocks and trusted contracts
Oil, gas and coal are Secure for resilience: they are essential and imported, and their supply takes one to three years to rebuild.

Size strategic stocks to that time, reserve capacity with trusted producers such as the United States, Canada and Norway for oil (partner evidence is weak, so test the contract terms), and stress-test the loss of the largest supplier.
Catch up in battery materials and components with time-limited support tied to benchmarks

Tie production incentives, first-of-a-kind finance, workforce and supplier development and demand creation to benchmarks, with sunsets, and keep the gate open to licensing and joint ventures that transfer capability.
Build battery components at home where the base is established and with allied partners for the rest.
Turn mineral dependence into investment bargains with trusted producers

Buy battery and EV minerals through offtake and co-investment with producers such as Australia, the United States and Canada, with export-credit finance for their capacity and contracts spread across several suppliers.
Build trusted battery and wind capacity with developing partners
Start with the Philippines in battery materials refining and Indonesia in battery components.
Test Viet Nam in wind turbines first, where the data record no operating or committed plant and the step's trade codes also cover cables, substations and transformers.
Prepare India in rare-earth and wind materials refining over a longer horizon.
Use project preparation, infrastructure and skills where the constraint is a public good, and development finance, guarantees and offtake where it is bankability.
Accelerate nuclear, solar and wind while keeping sourcing open

Deploy faster through infrastructure, permitting and procurement; buy commodity hardware competitively from trusted suppliers, and attach trusted-supplier and security conditions to public deployment support and to equipment with built-in control.
Every number comes from the Country page data of the Allied Industrial Base Explorer (the data release of 30 October 2026) and from the Allied Industrial Base analysis.
Each technology is split into supply-chain stages from extraction to recycling, and each step gets a strategic choice by fixed rules applied in order:
Secure where an acute vulnerability is measured;
at deployment, Accelerate where deployment need reaches 60;
Watch where the step is a large, commoditized yard;
Preserve where Competitive Position is in the top quarter (75) and either Strategic Industrial Value (bar 60) or supply-chain need (bar 67) is high;
Catch Up where the value is high, the position is not, and a capability anchor is corroborated by other evidence;
Partner where supply-chain need is high but there is neither a top-quarter position nor, for a high-value step, a credible pathway;
Named layers inside a step, such as control software or magnets, take their own choice, and a step whose parts sit behind different fences is mixed.
A value that rests on market size alone is capped just under the bar.
Observed policy never decides a choice.

The high fence (Secure) protects what cannot be allowed to fail; the medium fence covers capabilities worth building, keeping or sourcing deliberately and deployment to accelerate; the low fence (Watch) leaves a step open to competitive purchase.
Some calls rest on low confidence, an engine review flag, a thin capability anchor, a known data artifact or, at deployment, a single indicator of low confidence.
They stay on the map but never enter the Bottom line, the Agenda, the policy table or a headline mark.
For Japan several sit close to the top-quarter bar, where the line between Preserve and Catch Up is thin.
